title: The platform economy (Uber, Airbnb...)
subtitle: Capitalism without factories
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Uber, Airbnb and Deliveroo own almost nothing: no cars, no apartments, no employees. How did these platforms become global giants?

hero.hook: Uber has never owned a single car, and it still turned transport upside down all over the world.

blocks.text: Uber, Airbnb, Amazon and Deliveroo belong to a new kind of company: the **digital platform**. They do not simply put existing services online. They change what it means to own, to work and to be protected.
This model has invented a new form of capitalism, one that puts our social contract in question. Let us look at how it works, and why it causes so much argument.

A traditional company owns factories, vehicles and stock, and it employs staff. A platform breaks that model. It becomes a simple piece of digital infrastructure that connects supply and demand, without producing anything itself.

The system runs on the [[network effect]]: the more users a platform has, the more useful it becomes, which attracts still more users. For a ride service, the more drivers are available, the shorter the wait, which brings in more customers, who in turn bring in more drivers. That circle almost always ends in something close to a monopoly.
Uber has spent billions of dollars on self-driving car research, with the long-term aim of getting rid of its last big cost: the human driver.

sections.title: Work without the protections of employment

blocks.text: That technical innovation comes with a legal one that is far more contested. This is the world of the [[gig economy and uberization]]: the platform refuses the role of employer and presents itself as a simple technology middleman, which spares it social contributions, a minimum wage and paid vacation.

blocks.caption: Drivers and couriers are often classified as self-employed rather than as staff

blocks.text: The worker becomes a contractor who carries every risk alone: illness, accident, a drop in demand. Yet the rules of the app still apply, from set fares to ratings and penalties, a situation known as **algorithmic subordination**. In response, courts in several countries have begun to order the [[Reclassification]] of these contracts as real jobs with employee status.

The impact of these platforms goes beyond the world of work. It reshapes cities too. By making short-term tourist rentals easy, Airbnb competes with traditional hotels while cutting the number of homes available to residents.

The result is rising rents in city centers, and cities like Paris and Barcelona have had to impose strict rules, such as caps on the number of nights a home can be rented. States are also trying to bring in **digital taxation**, so that these platforms pay their share of tax where they really earn their money.
In New York, strict regulation of Airbnb in 2023 cut the number of legal listings by 80% within a few months.

sections.title: Toward a new status for workers?

blocks.text: The platform economy has brought fast services that are often cheaper, and it has made it easier for some people to find an income. But that efficiency rests on weakening the protections built up over the 20th century.

The current debate is about creating an in-between status, somewhere between employee and contractor, with portable rights: every worker would build up social protection whatever the number of platforms they work for. The future of the model will depend on whether regulators can frame it without smothering innovation.

The platform economy rests on a capitalism without factories that exploits the network effect, while turning its workers into contractors who are often insecure. The fight for better social protection, without breaking the model, is only beginning.
